title: Eagle County Wells: Depth, Yield and Drilling Cost
meta_description: Eagle County wells have a median depth of 124 ft. Review local yields, water levels, drilling costs and checks before buying rural property.
h1: What to Expect From a Well in Eagle County
intro_html:
A well budget for property near Wolcott, Fulford or Red Cliff should start with nearby completion records, not a countywide average alone. Eagle County's median recorded well depth is 124 ft, but the middle half runs from 58-260 ft. That spread matters when pricing mountain drilling.

Colorado DWR records contain 4,665 permitted wells in the county, with 2,095 recorded as constructed. These are mixed-use records, including monitoring wells, rather than a survey of operating household supplies. Use the county figures to frame your questions, then narrow the search to the property.

sections.heading: Why Eagle County's 124 ft Median Is Only a Starting Point
sections.html:
Depth is reported for 2,455 wells. The median is 124 ft, and the middle half falls between 58-260 ft. For a drilling bid, that means a substantial range of possible footage even before considering unusually deep holes. The 90th-percentile depth is 400 ft; the median is not a stopping-depth guarantee.

Most permits fall in the unnamed / fractured-bedrock category, covering 4,527 wells, while 42 name Alluvial and 17 name Morrison. Mountain bedrock supplies depend on intersecting productive fractures. A nearby well can guide expectations without predicting the result on your lot. Compare records around Edwards or McCoy with similar terrain and recorded geology, not simply the nearest address.

sections.heading: Reported Yields Look Strong, but Test the Household Supply
sections.html:
Among 933 wells reporting pump yield, the median is 15.0 gpm and the middle half is 12.0-15.0 gpm. Those reported rates look encouraging for household supply, but a completion-record yield is not proof that a well can maintain that output through sustained use.

The low end still deserves attention: 1% report under 1 gpm, and 4% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. A buyer facing low production may need storage and careful demand management. Before closing on a home near Eagle or Gypsum, obtain a pumping and recovery test. Confirm permitted uses separately; physical production does not authorize irrigation or other outdoor demand.

sections.heading: Eagle County Water Levels Do Not Show a Steady Decline
sections.html:
Static water level is the resting depth to water, not the bottom of the well. The 304 records reporting it have a median of 40 ft below ground, with the middle half at 20-114 ft. A shallow resting level does not establish how much water the well can produce under pumping.

Decade medians move from 26 ft in the 1970s to 66 ft in the 2000s, then back to 38 ft in the 2020s. That is not a steady countywide deepening trend. These measurements also come from different wells and locations, not repeated readings at a fixed monitoring network. For a particular property, ask for its own water-level and pumping history.

sections.heading: The County's Permit Boom and Recorded Drillers
sections.html:
The largest permit decade in Eagle County's record is the 1990s, with 1,448 permits. Issuance then totals 766 in the 2000s, 478 in the 2010s and 305 in the 2020s, with the newest permit dated 2026. The current decade is incomplete, and permits should not be treated as completed wells.

Golden Eagle Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Joe Wayne) appears on 772 records, and Shelton Drilling Corporation (Shelton, Wayne) on 739. Those historical counts do not establish present availability. Domestic/household uses account for 56% of records, while monitoring accounts for 26%. When comparing a property in Avon or Minturn, separate household supplies from monitoring installations.

sections.heading: Budgeting a New Well in Eagle County Mountain Ground
sections.html:
The local cost model assumes fractured mountain bedrock, including granite and gneiss, at $65-$100 per foot. At the 124 ft median depth, the drilled hole is about $8,100-$12,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is modeled at $14,100-$24,400.

Treat those figures as planning allowances, not a parcel quote. The 58-260 ft middle-half depth range explains why bids need clear footage pricing and a plan for additional drilling. Ask what casing, grout and well development are included. On a mountain lot near Vail or Fulford, rig access and the route between the well and house also deserve a site visit before committing to a budget.

sections.heading: Mine Features, PFAS Flags and Low-Yield Risk
sections.html:
The mapped environmental screening includes 25 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 44 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. These are reasons to investigate the parcel's surroundings, not evidence that its well is contaminated. A PFAS sampling location alone does not establish a detection in your water.

Have the water tested for household suitability, and use nearby site histories to discuss additional laboratory testing. Inspect casing, the sanitary seal and surface drainage. Fractured rock can produce sharply different results between neighboring lots, so discuss an unsuccessful-hole contingency with the driller. Coordinate the well location with septic approval, the building footprint and access before excavation begins.

sections.heading: Before Buying Land From Basalt to Dotsero
sections.html:
Start with the property's DWR permit, completion report and pump record. Confirm that the permitted use matches your plans; an exempt household-use permit does not automatically allow landscape watering or livestock. In an over-appropriated basin, proposed uses may require an augmentation plan. Resolve the water-supply path before treating vacant land as buildable.

Then compare nearby constructed wells around Basalt, Dotsero or the relevant community, checking depth, yield and recorded geology. County medians are background, not a parcel appraisal. For an existing home, make water quality and pumping performance part of due diligence. For a new build, have the driller and site contractor review access, septic placement, utilities and the house location together.

faq.q: How deep are wells in Eagle County, Colorado?
faq.a: The median recorded depth is 124 ft, based on 2,455 wells with depth information. The middle half runs from 58-260 ft, and the 90th percentile is 400 ft. Fractured mountain bedrock makes individual results variable, so use nearby completion reports to refine expectations before accepting a drilling allowance.

faq.q: How much does it cost to drill a well in Eagle County?
faq.a: The Eagle County model uses $65-$100 per foot for fractured mountain bedrock. At the median depth of 124 ft, drilling alone is about $8,100-$12,400. A finished well with pump, tank, trenching and electrical is about $14,100-$24,400. Get a parcel-specific quote covering access, casing, grout and additional footage.

faq.q: How much water do wells produce in Eagle County?
faq.a: Reported pump yield has a median of 15.0 gpm, with the middle half at 12.0-15.0 gpm across 933 records. Still, 1% report under 1 gpm and 4% fall in the 1-5 gpm band. For a home purchase, test sustained pumping and recovery rather than relying only on the original reported yield.

faq.q: Is well water safe to drink in Eagle County?
faq.a: County permit data cannot establish drinking-water safety at a particular house. The mapped screening includes 25 PFAS sampling/contamination sites, 44 historic mine features and 7 EPA Superfund/cleanup sites within about 10 miles. Proximity is not proof of contamination. Test the property's water and choose additional analyses based on nearby environmental records.

faq.q: Is the water table dropping in Eagle County?
faq.a: The available decade medians do not show a steady decline. Resting water depth increased from 26 ft in the 1970s to 66 ft in the 2000s, then decreased to 38 ft in the 2020s. These are different groups of wells, not a continuous monitoring record. Check the property's own measurement history.
